idiom_name: Validate() error checked at the call site, sync.OnceValue for a one-shot gate
implementation_notes: Go has no constructors and no exceptions, so validity is always decided at the point of use: the idiom is a Validate() error or ValidateForPublish() error method that the consuming function calls before the irreversible step, and the error value is the whole reporting channel - callers wrap it with fmt.Errorf("%w") or accumulate several with errors.Join. When the check is expensive and the object is immutable after build, sync.OnceValue (Go 1.21) or sync.OnceFunc memoises it so the first caller pays and everyone after sees the same result. A validator type with injected rules earns its keep only when the rule set is shared across types; otherwise the method plus the error value replaces the classic validator structure entirely.
pitfalls: sync.OnceValue memoises failure as well as success and sync.OnceFunc replays a panic on every later call, so a transient validation failure becomes permanent for that object.
Every struct literal is a constructor: the zero value of an Order is always reachable unvalidated, so the gate has to sit at each exit from the component rather than at one official entry point.
errors.Join accumulates context but hides the original type, so if callers must branch on a specific failure keep the sentinel error and join only additional detail.
